1. A magnetized needle is oscillating on a string about a vertical axis in a horizontal magnetic field $B$. The time for 10 oscillations is recorded for different values of $B$.
[Diagram: magnetized needle suspended horizontally from a vertical string in a horizontal magnetic field (arrows)]
The graph shows the variation with $B$ of the time for 10 oscillations together with the uncertainties in the time measurements. The uncertainty in $B$ is negligible.
[Graph: time for 10 oscillations / s (4 to 11) against B / T (0 to 0.020); eight data points with vertical error bars, decreasing from about 10.4 s at B = 0.003 T to about 4.4 s at B = 0.018 T]
(a) Draw on the graph the line of best fit for the data. [1]
(b) (i) Write down the time taken for one oscillation when $B = 0.005\,\text{T}$ with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
(ii) A student forms a hypothesis that the period of one oscillation $P$ is given by: $P = \frac{K}{\sqrt{B}}$ where $K$ is a constant.
Determine the value of $K$ using the point for which $B = 0.005\,\text{T}$. State the uncertainty in $K$ to an appropriate number of significant figures. [3]
(iii) State the unit of $K$. [1]
(c) The student plots a graph to show how $P^2$ varies with $\frac{1}{B}$ for the data.
Sketch the shape of the expected line of best fit on the axes below assuming that the relationship $P = \frac{K}{\sqrt{B}}$ is verified. You do not have to put numbers on the axes. [2]
[Blank axes: $P^2$ against $\frac{1}{B}$, origin 0]
(d) State how the value of $K$ can be obtained from the graph. [1]

2. An experiment to find the internal resistance of a cell of known emf is to be set. The following equipment is available:
[Circuit symbols: one cell; one ammeter; 10 Ω resistor]
(a) Draw a suitable circuit diagram that would enable the internal resistance to be determined. [1]
(b) It is noticed that the resistor gets warmer. Explain how this would affect the calculated value of the internal resistance. [3]
(c) Outline how using a variable resistance could improve the accuracy of the value found for the internal resistance. [2]

3.text_clean:
3. The diagram shows the motion of the electrons in a metal wire carrying an electric current as seen by an observer X at rest with respect to the wire. The distance between adjacent positive charges is $d$.
[Diagram: section of wire with a row of electrons (−) moving to the left above a row of stationary positive charges (+) separated by distance d]
(a) State whether the field around the wire according to observer X is electric, magnetic or a combination of both. [1]
(b) Observer Y is at rest with respect to the electrons.
(i) Discuss the change in $d$ according to observer Y. [2]
(ii) Deduce whether the overall field around the wire is electric, magnetic or a combination of both according to observer Y. [2]

4.text_clean:
4. Muons are created in the upper atmosphere of the Earth at an altitude of 10 km above the surface. The muons travel vertically down at a speed of $0.995c$ with respect to the Earth. When measured at rest the average lifetime of the muons is $2.1\,\mu\text{s}$.
(a) (i) Calculate, according to Galilean relativity, the time taken for a muon to travel to the ground. [1]
(ii) Deduce why only a small fraction of the total number of muons created is expected to be detected at ground level according to Galilean relativity. [1]
(b) (i) Calculate, according to the theory of special relativity, the time taken for a muon to reach the ground in the reference frame of the muon. [2]
(ii) Discuss how your result in (b)(i) and the outcome of the muon decay experiment support the theory of special relativity. [2]

5.text_clean:
5. An observer on Earth watches rocket A travel away from Earth at a speed of $0.80c$. The spacetime diagram shows the worldline of rocket A in the frame of reference of the Earth observer who is at rest at $x = 0$.
[Spacetime diagram: ct / km (0 to 4) against x / km (−2 to 2); worldline of A is a straight line from the origin to about (2, 2.5)]
Another rocket, B, departs from the same location as A but later than A at $ct = 1.2\,\text{km}$ according to the Earth observer. Rocket B travels at a constant speed of $0.60c$ in the opposite direction to A according to the Earth observer.
(a) Draw on the spacetime diagram the worldline of B according to the Earth observer and label it B. [2]
Rocket A and rocket B both emit a flash of light that are received simultaneously by the Earth observer. Rocket A emits the flash of light at a time coordinate $ct = 1.8\,\text{km}$ according to the Earth observer.
(b) Deduce, showing your working on the spacetime diagram, the value of $ct$ according to the Earth observer at which the rocket B emitted its flash of light. [3]
(c) Explain whether or not the arrival times of the two flashes in the Earth frame are simultaneous events in the frame of rocket A. [2]
(d) Calculate the velocity of rocket B relative to rocket A. [2]

6.text_clean:
6. A positive pion decays into a positive muon and a neutrino.
$\pi^+ \rightarrow \mu^+ + \nu_\mu$
The momentum of the muon is measured to be $29.8\,\text{MeV}\,c^{-1}$ in a laboratory reference frame in which the pion is at rest. The rest mass of the muon is $105.7\,\text{MeV}\,c^{-2}$ and the mass of the neutrino can be assumed to be zero.
(a) For the laboratory reference frame
(i) write down the momentum of the neutrino. [1]
(ii) show that the energy of the pion is about 140 MeV. [2]
(b) State the rest mass of the pion with an appropriate unit. [1]

7.text_clean:
7. An observer A is on the surface of planet X. Observer B is in a stationary spaceship above the surface of planet X.
Observer A sends a beam of light with a frequency 500 THz towards observer B. When observer B receives the light he observes that the frequency has changed by $\Delta f$.
[Diagram: observer A on the surface of planet X sends 500 THz light upwards to observer B in a spaceship above]
Observer B then sends a signal with frequency 1500 THz towards observer A.
[Diagram: observer B in the spaceship sends 1500 THz signal down to observer A on planet X]
(a) Calculate the shift in frequency observed by A in terms of $\Delta f$. [2]
(b) Calculate the gravitational field strength on the surface of planet X.
The following data is given: $\Delta f = 170\,\text{Hz}$.
The distance between observer A and B is 10 km. [2]
(c) Observer A now sends a beam of light initially parallel to the surface of the planet.
[Diagram: observer A on planet X with a beam of light directed horizontally]
Explain why the path of the light is curved. [2]

8.text_clean:
8. A constant force of 50.0 N is applied tangentially to the outer edge of a merry-go-round. The following diagram shows the view from above.
[Diagram: circle of diameter 4.00 m with a tangential force of 50.0 N at its edge]
The merry-go-round has a moment of inertia of $450\,\text{kg m}^2$ about a vertical axis. The merry-go-round has a diameter of 4.00 m.
(a) Show that the angular acceleration of the merry-go-round is $0.2\,\text{rad s}^{-2}$. [2]
(b) The merry-go-round starts from rest and the force is applied for one complete revolution.
Calculate, for the merry-go-round after one revolution,
(i) the angular speed. [1]
(ii) the angular momentum. [1]
A child of mass 30.0 kg is now placed onto the edge of the merry-go-round. No external torque acts on the system.
(c) Calculate the new angular speed of the rotating system. [2]
(d) The child now moves towards the centre.
(i) Explain why the angular speed will increase. [2]
(ii) Calculate the work done by the child in moving from the edge to the centre. [2]

9.text_clean:
9. The pressure–volume ($pV$) diagram shows a cycle ABCA of a heat engine. The working substance of the engine is 0.221 mol of ideal monatomic gas.
[pV diagram (not to scale): A at V = 5.00 × 10⁻³ m³ (low pressure); adiabatic curve from A to B at V = 2.00 × 10⁻³ m³; isobaric B to C at V = 5.00 × 10⁻³ m³; isochoric C to A]
At A the temperature of the gas is 295 K and the pressure of the gas is $1.10 \times 10^5\,\text{Pa}$. The process from A to B is adiabatic.
(a) Show that the pressure at B is about $5 \times 10^5\,\text{Pa}$. [2]
(b) For the process BC, calculate, in J,
(i) the work done by the gas. [1]
(ii) the change in the internal energy of the gas. [1]
(iii) the thermal energy transferred to the gas. [1]
(c) The process from B to C is replaced by an isothermal process in which the initial state is the same and the final volume is $5.00 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3$.
(i) Explain, without any calculation, why the pressure after this change would be lower if the process was isothermal. [2]
(ii) Determine, without any calculation, whether the net work done by the engine during one full cycle would increase or decrease. [2]
(d) Outline why an efficiency calculation is important for an engineer designing a heat engine. [1]

10. The water supply for a hydroelectric plant is a reservoir with a large surface area. An outlet pipe takes the water to a turbine.
[Diagram: reservoir behind a dam; outlet pipe runs down to a turbine at height H below the water level]
(a) State the difference in terms of the velocity of the water between laminar and turbulent flow. [1]
(b) The water level is a height $H$ above the turbine. Assume that the flow is laminar in the outlet pipe.
Show, using the Bernoulli equation, that the speed of the water as it enters the turbine is given by $v = \sqrt{2gH}$. [3]
(c) The following data are available:
density of water $= 1.00 \times 10^3\,\text{kg m}^{-3}$
viscosity of water $= 1.31 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{Pa s}$
diameter of the outlet pipe $= 0.600\,\text{m}$
velocity of water at outlet pipe $= 59.4\,\text{m s}^{-1}$
(i) Calculate the Reynolds number for the water flow. [1]
(ii) Outline whether it is reasonable to assume that flow is laminar in this situation. [1]

[Graph: x / m (−1 to 1) against t / s (0 to 13); oscillation of period 2 s whose amplitude decreases gradually from about 0.8 m at t = 0]
(a) Describe the motion of the spring-mass system. [1]

12. (a) A converging (convex) lens forms an image of an object on a screen.
[Diagram (not to scale): object, converging lens and screen on a principal axis]
(i) Identify whether the image is real or virtual. [1]
(ii) The lens is 18 cm from the screen and the image is 0.40 times smaller than the object. Calculate the power of the lens, in $\text{cm}^{-1}$. [3]
(iii) Light passing through this lens is subject to chromatic aberration. Discuss the effect that chromatic aberration has on the image formed on the screen. [3]
(b) A system consisting of a converging lens of focal length $F_1$ (lens 1) and a diverging lens (lens 2) are used to obtain the image of an object as shown on the scaled diagram. The focal length of lens 1 ($F_1$) is 30 cm.
[Scaled ray diagram on a grid (scale: one square = 10 cm): object, lens 1 and lens 2 a short distance apart, focal points F1 either side of lens 1, inverted final image to the right]
Determine, using the ray diagram, the focal length of the diverging lens. [3]

[Diagram: ray in the core of an optic fibre totally internally reflected at point P on the core–cladding boundary]
The refractive index of the core is 1.56 and that of the cladding 1.34.
(a) Calculate the critical angle at the core−cladding boundary. [1]
(b) The use of optical fibres has led to a revolution in communications across the globe. Outline two advantages of optical fibres over electrical conductors for the purpose of data transfer. [2]

[Graph: intensity / arbitrary units (0 to 1.25) against wavelength / nm (100 to 1000); continuous spectrum peaking at about 290 nm with small absorption dips near 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm]
The second graph shows the hydrogen emission spectrum in the visible range.

19. A galaxy can be modelled as a sphere of radius $R_0$. The distance of a star from the centre of the galaxy is $r$.
[Graph: mass enclosed against r; rises from 0 to M at r = R0, then constant at M]
For this model the graph is a simplified representation of the variation with $r$ of the mass of visible matter enclosed inside $r$.
(a) The mass of visible matter in the galaxy is $M$.
Show that for stars where $r > R_0$ the velocity of orbit is $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$. [1]
(b) Draw on the axes the observed variation with $r$ of the orbital speed $v$ of stars in a galaxy. [2]
[Blank axes: v against r, with R0 marked]
